h1: The 6 Best Printers for Documents of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Documents: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six printers for text and document printing in 2026, covering laser and inkjet, duplex, document feeders and ink costs.
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer for documents: monochrome laser, automatic duplex and toner that fuses to the page. Choose the Canon MF753Cdw II if you need color at 35 ppm with a feeder. The Brother HL-L3220CDW is the cheaper color laser, while the HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e is the low-cost inkjet. The PIXMA TR4720 is only for fax.
intro: Printer marketing is built around color gamuts and borderless photos, yet the typical home office prints contracts, tax forms and school reports in black. That mismatch is why so many buyers end up with an inkjet that clogs after a quiet month and a cartridge bill that dwarfs the hardware price.

For paper documents the engine type and duplex capability decide almost everything. We reviewed six printers, laser and inkjet, and scored them on the Primea framework using listed engine, duplex, document feeder, speed and the way each handles ink or toner. Text sharpness and long-run cost counted most. Inkjets that only suit light use are flagged as such rather than hidden, because a cheap printer that sits unused for weeks usually costs more than it saves.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser Printer
products.verdict: A compact monochrome laser built for sharp, durable text.
products.description:
The DCP-L2640DW is a compact monochrome laser with duplex printing and wireless and mobile support. The mechanism is the point: laser toner is melted into the paper fibers, so letters stay crisp and do not feather the way inkjet ink can on cheap stock, and the output is listed as archivally stable.

It ranks first because it does the job most people buy a printer for and nothing else. The Canon MF753Cdw II prints faster and in color, but costs the same $200 to $500 tier and takes more desk space. If your pages are text, color capability is money spent on toner you will not use.

Buy it for contracts, reports and forms that must stay legible for years. The caveat is plain: black and white only, so charts and color graphics print in grayscale.
products.idealFor: Text-heavy documents that need to stay sharp and legible for years.

products.name: Canon Color imageCLASS MF753Cdw II Wireless Duplex Laser Printer
products.verdict: A 35 ppm color laser with an auto document feeder and a 3-year warranty.
products.description:
Canon's MF753Cdw II is the one here built for volume. It lists a 35 ppm color laser engine, duplex printing, an auto document feeder and a 3-year limited warranty, in the $200 to $500 tier.

That speed is nearly double the 19 ppm of the Brother HL-L3220CDW, and the feeder lets you copy or scan a stack of pages without standing at the glass. It sits second rather than first because most households never print enough to use the speed, and it is larger and costlier to feed than the monochrome Brother.

Buy it for a small office or busy family printing color handouts and text at real volume. Skip it if you print a few pages a week: you would pay for capacity that sits idle while four toner cartridges age.
products.idealFor: A household or small office needing sharp text plus color documents at real volume.
products.skipIf: You print only a few pages a week.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Wireless Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: A 19 ppm color laser with a 250-sheet tray and duplex.
products.description:
The HL-L3220CDW delivers color laser output at 19 ppm with a 250-sheet tray, duplex printing and mobile compatibility, also in the $200 to $500 tier. The tray capacity is the underrated spec: 250 sheets means reloading a few times a month rather than weekly.

It lands third because the Canon beats it on speed at 35 ppm and on the document feeder, which the Brother does not list. Against the DCP-L2640DW it adds color but gives up the lean text-only design. It occupies the middle: laser quality without the highest-end hardware.

Buy it for regular document output with occasional color. The caveat is that it is a printer only, so scanning or copying needs a separate device, which matters if you handle paperwork that arrives on paper.
products.idealFor: Regular document output that wants laser quality without the highest-end price.
products.skipIf: You need scanning or a feeder.

products.name: Brother INKvestment MCF-J5010DW Wireless Color Inkjet All-in-One
products.verdict: An inkjet with high-capacity INKvestment cartridges and automatic 2-sided copy and scan.
products.description:
The MCF-J5010DW is an inkjet built around INKvestment high-capacity cartridges, which cut how often you swap ink. It adds automatic 2-sided copy and scan, a 2.7-inch color touchscreen and wireless color printing, in the $200 to $500 tier.

It ranks fourth because it costs as much as the lasers above while its text is less durable: inkjet ink sits on the surface more than toner does. Its argument is flexibility. It handles photos and mixed pages that a monochrome laser cannot, and two-sided scanning is rare among picks here.

Buy it for a higher-volume home office that wants copy and scan tools plus color. Skip it if lowest cost per text page is the goal, since the Brother DCP-L2640DW wins that fight on a pure text workload.
products.idealFor: Higher-volume document printing that still wants inkjet color flexibility.
products.skipIf: You want lowest cost per text page.

products.name: HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A $50-100 inkjet with an auto document feeder and duplex.
products.description:
The OfficeJet Pro 8125e shows how far inkjets have come on features: an auto document feeder, duplex printing, AI-enabled setup and a 3-month Instant Ink trial, for the $50 to $100 tier. A feeder at that price is unusual.

It ranks fifth because the cheap hardware is the start of the spending, not the end. Ink costs accumulate, and the Instant Ink trial only softens them for three months, so check the subscription terms before enrolling. The MCF-J5010DW above it spends more on the printer in exchange for fewer cartridge swaps.

Buy it for mixed text and color at modest volume, particularly if you want to scan multi-page documents cheaply. Skip it if you print large amounts of plain text, where a laser runs cheaper over a year.
products.idealFor: Mixed text and color document printing without a laser's upfront cost.
products.skipIf: You print heavy volumes of text.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: A basic wireless all-in-one with a document feeder and built-in fax.
products.description:
The PIXMA TR4720 exists for one reason: it is the only pick here with built-in fax. It also has an auto document feeder, mobile printing support and wireless all-in-one functions, in the $50 to $100 tier, on standard cartridges.

It ranks last because it lists no duplex mode, which every other printer in this guide offers, and standard cartridges deplete faster than the high-capacity INKvestment type on the Brother MCF-J5010DW. The feeder and fax make it useful for paperwork that still arrives by phone line, but it is a light-duty machine.

Buy it for occasional scanning, copying and fax on a tight budget. Heavy printers will outgrow it quickly, and without duplex every double-sided job means flipping pages by hand.
products.idealFor: Budget document scanning and printing with occasional multi-page needs.

whatMatters.detail: Laser printers fuse toner into the paper with heat, giving sharp text that resists smearing, while inkjets spray liquid ink that costs less upfront and more per page. For mostly text, the engine matters more than any feature. Check that the title or spec table says laser, as the Brother DCP-L2640DW and Canon MF753Cdw II do.

Duplex means automatic two-sided printing. It halves paper use and lets you print booklets and long reports without flipping pages. Without it, every double-sided job needs manual reloading. Look for "duplex" or "2-sided" in the specs. The PIXMA TR4720 is the pick here with no listed duplex, which is a real daily irritation.

An auto document feeder pulls sheets through the scanner one at a time, so a ten page contract scans without lifting the lid ten times. If you copy or scan multi-page files, it is essential. The Canon MF753Cdw II, HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e and PIXMA TR4720 list one. Confirm it in the specs, not the photos.

Pages per minute tells you how long a long document takes to finish. The picks range from 19 ppm on the Brother HL-L3220CDW to 35 ppm on the Canon MF753Cdw II, where listed. Speed matters more for offices than households, since one slow printer queues everyone behind a long job. Look for the ppm figure in the title or spec table.

Consumables are the real cost. High-capacity cartridges like Brother's INKvestment mean fewer replacements, and laser toner lasts far longer than inkjet ink between purchases. Subscriptions such as HP's Instant Ink change the math too. Check how the listing describes cartridge capacity, and read the terms of any ink plan before enrolling, because a subscription can lock you into one cartridge supplier.

cards.text: Duplex printing, a wireless connection and toner that does not fade or smear.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Brother DCP-L2640DW lists duplex, wireless and mobile printing, plus smear-free toner.

cards.text: You print many pages or need color and a feeder. The Canon MF753Cdw II offers 35 ppm and a 3-year warranty.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You print little. The HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e and Canon PIXMA TR4720 sit in the $50-100 range.

faq.a: Usually yes, for text. Toner fuses to the page for sharp, non-feathering text, as on the Brother DCP-L2640DW, and it avoids the clogged nozzles inkjets suffer after quiet weeks. If you print color regularly, the Canon MF753Cdw II keeps the laser benefits.

Buying on color and photo features when you print mostly black text. You then pay for inkjet cartridges you barely use, and clogged nozzles after quiet weeks make it worse. A monochrome laser like the Brother DCP-L2640DW costs less to run for documents.

faq.q: Is the Canon MF753Cdw II worth it over the Brother HL-L3220CDW?
faq.a: If you need a document feeder and 35 ppm speed, yes. The Brother HL-L3220CDW is slower at 19 ppm and lists no feeder, so it suits lighter use with a 250-sheet tray.

faq.q: How do I set up wireless printing?
faq.a: Connect the printer to your Wi-Fi from its control panel or maker's app, then add it from your computer or phone, keeping both on the same network during setup. The HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e lists AI-enabled setup to guide you through it.

faq.q: How do I cut ink costs?
faq.a: Choose a laser such as the Brother DCP-L2640DW, or high-capacity cartridges like Brother INKvestment on the MCF-J5010DW. Print duplex to halve paper use, and avoid cheap standard cartridges, which the PIXMA TR4720 uses.

faq.q: Do I need a printer with a feeder?
faq.a: Only if you scan or copy multi-page documents regularly. The Canon MF753Cdw II, HP OfficeJet Pro 8125e and PIXMA TR4720 list one, while the Brother DCP-L2640DW and HL-L3220CDW suit pure printing.

finalTake: For documents, the Brother DCP-L2640DW is the right default: sharp laser text, automatic duplex and wireless printing in a compact body. Add the Canon MF753Cdw II when you need color at 35 ppm and a feeder. The Brother HL-L3220CDW is the cheaper color laser. Inkjets like the OfficeJet Pro 8125e save money upfront but cost more per page of text.
